common_name: Georgian Crystal Garlic (Large-Clove Mild Porcelain Hardneck)

planting.note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Georgian Crystal is a porcelain hardneck that needs a real winter chill for good bulb formation and performs best in zone 3-7.

directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Georgian Crystal is a porcelain-type hardneck garlic originating in the country of Georgia, valued for its large, glossy white bulbs with just 4-6 very large cloves that are quick and easy to peel, along with a mild-to-medium, clean garlic flavor that works well both raw and cooked. It is a vigorous, reliable producer that adapts well across a range of cold-winter climates. Like other hardnecks, it sends up a curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to direct energy into bulb growth; scapes are excellent sautéed or made into pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot, then trim and store; storage life is moderate, typically 5-7 months in a cool, dry location.
sources: Chester Aaron: The Great Garlic Book, Ten Speed Press 1997

common_name: Duganski Garlic (Spicy Russian Purple Stripe Hardneck)

planting.note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Duganski is a purple stripe hardneck that needs a real winter chill for good bulb formation and performs best in zone 3-7.

directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Duganski is a purple stripe hardneck garlic originally from Russia, valued for its notably strong, hot, spicy raw flavor that mellows into a rich, robust taste when roasted or cooked, making it a favorite among gardeners who want an assertive, full-flavored garlic. Bulbs have deep reddish-purple streaked skin over 8-10 tightly packed cloves. As a hardneck, it sends up a curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to focus the plant's energy on bulb development; scapes are tender and flavorful when harvested young. Duganski also stores somewhat better than many other purple stripe types, often holding for 6-8 months in a cool, dry location. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, then cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot before trimming.
sources: Chester Aaron: The Great Garlic Book, Ten Speed Press 1997
